question: Which of the following best defines the clinically critical difference between neurotic and psychotic disorders?

answers.text: Neurotic disorders are caused by psychological stressors; psychotic disorders are always caused by biological factors.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Aetiology alone does not define the neurotic-psychotic divide; both categories can have biological and psychological contributions.

answers.text: In psychotic disorders, reality testing is fundamentally impaired; in neurotic disorders, the patient retains contact with shared reality.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The core distinction is loss of reality testing in psychosis — the patient cannot distinguish internal experiences (hallucinations, delusional beliefs) from external reality — whereas neurotic patients retain this capacity and typically experience distress about their symptoms.

answers.text: Neurotic disorders always require psychotherapy; psychotic disorders always require antipsychotics.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Treatment modality is not the defining criterion; the distinction is phenomenological (reality testing), not prescriptive.

answers.text: Psychotic disorders are more severe and therefore require inpatient care, while neurotic disorders are always managed in outpatient settings.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Severity of care setting is not the defining criterion. Severe neurotic disorders (e.g., severe OCD with suicidality) can require inpatient admission.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the neurotic-psychotic dichotomy section. The key is phenomenological: psychosis involves impaired reality testing; neurosis preserves it.
Well done. Reality testing — the capacity to distinguish internal mental experiences from external reality — is the conceptual anchor of the neurotic-psychotic dichotomy.
